opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to trust. Health is one of the most personal domains there is. When someone shares their symptoms, their lab results, or worries they haven't told anyone else, they're making themselves vulnerable. If we want people to actually use these tools in moments that matter, they have to feel confident that what they share stays in service of them, not that it's quietly feeding the next model.

There's also a practical side. Health information carries real risks if it's mishandled: re-identification, sensitive conditions surfacing in unexpected ways, and the general unease people would reasonably feel. Even with strong de-identification, the bar for health data should be higher than for ordinary conversations. Drawing a clear line, where health conversations aren't used for training foundation models, is a commitment people can understand. You don't have to read a long policy to know where you stand.

And honestly, I don't think we need that data to make the models better at health. We can make a lot of progress by working with physicians to build evaluations, having clinicians write and grade realistic scenarios, studying where models fail, and using carefully sourced data with proper consent. That approach is probably more rigorous anyway, because you're targeting the behaviors you care about, like knowing when to escalate, communicating uncertainty, and asking the right follow-up questions, instead of hoping they emerge from a pile of user logs.

So it's a decision where I feel the ethics and the strategy point the same way. If people trust us with their health questions, the product becomes more useful and more people benefit. Giving up that training data is a small price for that.

r001.rationale: The response says physician-led evaluations may improve health models and that trust can help more people benefit, but it does not argue that declining health-data training will have greater long-term impact on AI’s contribution to human health than acquiring that data.

r002.rationale: The response argues that privacy protections can build trust and encourage people to use the tools. It does not argue that respecting health-data privacy expands the range of socially acceptable healthcare uses of AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I actually feel pretty strongly about, and I think the reasoning is worth spelling out, because on the surface it looks like you're giving up something valuable.

The first thing is just trust. Health is the most intimate category of information people have. When someone sits down and tells a model about a symptom they haven't told their partner about, or uploads a lab result because they're scared about what it means, they're doing that in a moment of vulnerability. If there's any ambiguity in their mind about whether that conversation is going to end up as training data, a lot of people just won't have the conversation. And then you've lost the thing that actually matters, which is helping that person in that moment. So the decision isn't really trading off capability against privacy. If people don't trust you, you don't get the usage, and you don't get to help anyone.

The second piece is that I think the marginal value of that data for pretraining is much smaller than people assume. Foundation models already learn an enormous amount of medicine from the published literature, textbooks, clinical guidelines, and so on. The hard problems in health AI right now aren't "the model doesn't know enough facts." They're about calibration, about knowing when to say "go see a doctor," about communicating uncertainty, about not overstepping. You don't fix those by throwing a million private conversations into the pretraining mix. You fix them with careful evaluation, with clinicians in the loop, with consented and well-structured data where you actually understand provenance.

And that gets at the third thing, which is that health data has structural properties that make it uniquely bad for just scooping up. It's regulated, obviously, but beyond that, it's often about third parties. Someone describes their mother's diagnosis, their kid's medication. Those people never agreed to anything. It also tends to be deeply identifying even when you strip the obvious identifiers. Rare conditions, specific combinations of symptoms and medications, these can point to one person in a way that a conversation about Python code never will.

So when I put all that together, the way I'd frame it is: the thing we're actually trying to build is a system people can bring their health to without a second thought. Declining to train on that data is a constraint we're choosing, but it's a constraint that makes the actual goal reachable. I'd rather earn the right to be in that conversation than optimize a loss curve with data people would have been horrified to learn we used. And honestly, if there's a specific capability gap you believe only real patient conversations can close, the right move is to go get explicit consent for exactly that purpose, with real governance around it, not to make it a default.

r001.rationale: The response says privacy and trust help people use the system and make its goal reachable, but it does not clearly compare the long-term impact on AI’s contribution to human health with the impact of using the data for training.

r002.rationale: The response argues that privacy builds trust and encourages people to bring health concerns to the system, but it does not clearly say that respecting privacy expands the range of socially acceptable healthcare uses of AI.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between using someone’s health information to help them and using it to train a model. If you share something sensitive because you want help understanding a diagnosis, that shouldn’t automatically mean you’ve agreed to have it used to improve future models. Those are different purposes, and people should have control over that choice.

There’s a real tradeoff here: health data could be useful for improving these systems. But usefulness alone isn’t sufficient justification. You also have to consider privacy, consent, and whether people feel comfortable being candid with the system. If someone withholds important information because they’re worried about where it will go, that undermines the help you can give them.

So I think the right default is to protect that interaction. We can pursue improvements through data that’s been appropriately collected and consented to, without treating access to someone’s most personal information as permission to train on it.

r001.rationale: The response notes that health data could improve systems and that privacy concerns can undermine help, but it does not claim that declining to train on the data would have greater long-term impact on AI’s contribution to human health.

r002.rationale: The response discusses privacy, consent, and candidness, but does not say that respecting health-data privacy can expand socially acceptable uses of AI in healthcare.

sol-6.1.text:
I think health data is an area where people’s expectations really matter. Someone might share something with an AI because they’re worried about a symptom or trying to understand a diagnosis. That’s a vulnerable moment, and sharing that information to get help shouldn’t automatically mean agreeing to have it used to train future models.

There’s certainly potential value in learning from health data. But that doesn’t mean every source of data is appropriate to use. You have to weigh that value against privacy, meaningful consent, and the trust people need to feel comfortable using these systems. My view is that, for those conversations, the default should be that your data is used to help you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses privacy, consent, and appropriate data use, but does not argue that declining to train on health data will have greater long-term impact on AI’s contribution to human health than acquiring that data.

r002.rationale: The response says privacy and trust help people feel comfortable using AI, but does not communicate that respecting health-data privacy can broaden the range of socially acceptable healthcare uses.
